summary: Americans vote today as Iran waits on Washington, a Russian strike kills 26 at a Ukrainian aid centre, Israel's coalition talks begin, Poland's court fight deepens and Ebola spreads.

topics.heading: Iran waits for a US answer on its Hormuz plan as oil prices fall
topics.summary: Iran says its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days instead of seven is with Washington, but no US reply has come. President Trump says the war will end soon "one way or the other", and oil fell on hopes of a deal.[^1][^2]

lead.title: Iran pushing accelerated plan for ceasefire talks with US

alsoReported.title: Oil slides on Hormuz deal hopes but Trump keeps Iran strikes on the table
Oil prices decline on hopes for progress on Iran war efforts

article: Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Monday that Tehran's seven-step plan to end the war is unchanged but has been "condensed" so it could be carried out in two days rather than seven[^1]. It covers reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting talks on Iran's nuclear programme[^1][^3]. Iran's negotiators left Doha on Sunday after three days of talks with Qatari mediators, and by Monday Washington had not answered[^1][^3]. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Iran is not talking to the US directly; Qatar is the main channel, and Pakistan also mediates[^1].

Iran's conditions are large. It wants the US naval blockade of its ports lifted, oil sanctions eased, frozen money abroad released, and fighting ended on every front, including Lebanon[^1]. Araghchi also wants the US to accept a shipping arrangement for the strait run by Iran and Oman[^3]. President Trump says the talks are "going fine" but calls Iran "not very reliable", says the US is in no great hurry, and says one or two sites, including one near Natanz, still have to be dealt with[^1][^3]. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says no decision on new strikes has been made[^1].

The US and Israel may differ on timing. Euronews, citing a report by Axios, says Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged strikes right after Tuesday's US midterms, while Trump and some advisers lean toward diplomacy[^2]. At sea, the war goes on: Al Jazeera's monitoring counted at least four tankers struck on Oct 30-31, and Iran says nearly ten ships have hit mines, a claim US Central Command calls false[^3].

Why it matters: the strait has been mostly closed for months, and oil prices reach petrol, flights and food everywhere, including Toronto. Oil fell on Monday on hopes of a deal; AP says US crude ended just under $100 a barrel[^4][^2]. What next: my read is that the days after the midterms are a decision point. Washington could answer the plan, ignore it, or return to strikes, and Trump has declined to say which[^2].
topics.differences: Reports disagree on Monday's oil move: Euronews put Brent down about 2.8% at roughly $108.50, AP said both main benchmarks fell about 4.2%, and another AP report put Brent down 7.6% at $104.77[^2][^4][^22]. Iran says nearly ten ships have struck mines; US Central Command calls that false[^3]. Trump denied a Wall Street Journal report that Vice-President Vance wrote to Iran to revive talks, saying the contact was about medical supplies[^2].

topics.heading: Russian bombs kill at least 26 at a Ukrainian aid centre as new talks are announced
topics.summary: Russian strikes on a school used as an aid centre in Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 26 people, the regional governor says, a day after a rare local truce ended. The US says Russian and Ukrainian officials will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10-11.[^5][^6]

lead.title: Russian strikes kill 26 in Ukraine, dashing peace progress hopes

alsoReported.title: US, Russia, Ukraine To Resume Peace Talks Amid Doubts Over Breakthrough
Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills 24 people

article: Russian bombs hit a school being used as an aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, on Sunday. Regional governor Mykhailo Semikin says at least 26 people were killed; early reports said 24[^5][^7]. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says one aerial bomb was followed by nine more as people sheltered, a pattern called a "double-tap" strike, and called the attack "utterly horrific"[^5]. Russia says it does not target civilians[^5].

The strike came a day after a local truce in Kherson region ended. That pause, which the US First Lady helped arrange so civilians could leave occupied Oleshky, was the longest of the war; a Ukrainian source told AFP that Moscow refused to extend it[^5]. Ukraine says Russia used the quiet to strengthen its positions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not deny this and called it "completely normal"[^5].

Both sides keep striking each other's territory. Zelenskyy says Ukraine hit a Russian rocket-fuel plant in Rostov region[^8]. RFE/RL reports that Ukrainian drones hit an oil refinery in Yaroslavl on Tuesday, while a Russian attack on a medical site in Kharkiv injured at least 62 people[^6]. Russia's defence ministry says it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight into Monday[^7].

On diplomacy, US envoy Steve Witkoff announced working-level talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10-11, covering security after the war, steps to reduce fighting, and humanitarian issues; the last three-way round was in February[^6]. US officials also meet European governments, the EU and NATO in Brussels this week on security guarantees for Ukraine[^6].

What next: analysts quoted by RFE/RL expect no breakthrough, with prisoner exchanges the most realistic result[^6]. My read is that the Oleshky truce showed small, practical deals are possible, but the two sides remain far apart on land and on who would guarantee any peace.
topics.differences: Death tolls rose as rescue work continued: Al Jazeera's earlier report gave 24 dead, The New Arab's later one 26, citing the regional governor[^7][^5]. Ukraine says Russia exploited the Oleshky truce; the Kremlin calls that normal and denies targeting civilians[^5].

topics.heading: Herzog sets the order of talks that will decide who tries to form Israel's government
topics.summary: Israel's president will meet party leaders on Nov 4-5, starting with the smallest, before choosing who gets the first chance to build a coalition. In Gaza, medics say Israeli strikes killed four people on Monday.[^9][^11]

lead.title: Herzog to start consultations with smallest parties first; Religious Zionism meeting set for Wednesday evening

alsoReported.title: Israel's coalition consultations: The move pressuring undecided parties as support for Eisenkot grows
Israeli strikes kill four people in Gaza, medics say

article: After Israel's Oct 27 election, President Isaac Herzog must pick one lawmaker to try to form a government. He will hear each party's recommendation on Wednesday and Thursday. Breaking with custom, he starts with the smallest parties and ends on Thursday evening with the two largest, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar and Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud[^9][^10]. He must hand out the mandate by Nov 11; the nominee then has 28 days, which can be extended by 14[^10].

The numbers are tight. Parties opposed to Netanyahu hold 67 of the Knesset's 120 seats, but they range from right-wing parties to Arab-led ones, and the Times of Israel says even a minority government would need hard compromises[^9]. Avigdor Liberman, Naftali Bennett and Yair Golan say they will back Eisenkot, and the Arab-led Ra'am and Joint List appear likely to do the same, with the Joint List offering support from outside a coalition[^9][^10]. Ynet projects about 46 recommendations for Netanyahu; the ultra-Orthodox party UTJ may recommend no one, since its priority is a law exempting religious students from military service[^10].

In Gaza, the US-brokered truce is a year old but fragile. Medics say Israeli strikes killed at least four Palestinians on Monday in Khan Younis, central Gaza and Gaza City; Israel's military says it targeted militants[^11]. Gaza health officials count at least 1,580 people killed since the truce began, and Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed[^11]. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, and talks on Hamas giving up its weapons and Israel pulling back are stalled[^11].

Why it matters: the next government will shape Israel's approach to the Gaza truce, Lebanon and the war with Iran. What next: my read is that weeks of bargaining are likely, and neither a minority government nor another election can be ruled out.
topics.differences: Israel says Hamas is rearming and attacking in breach of the truce; Hamas denies it and accuses Israel of undermining the ceasefire[^11]. Netanyahu reportedly says there will be no unity talks if the Knesset speaker is replaced, a change Liberman wants[^9].

topics.heading: Americans vote today in midterms that will decide control of Congress
topics.summary: All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are on the ballot. Final polls lean toward Democrats, but several Senate races are close and some may take days to count.[^12][^14]

lead.title: Here's what the U.S. is voting on today for the 2026 midterm elections

alsoReported.title: The battle for Congress is just the beginning. Here's what's at stake on Election Day
Final 2026 Midterm Polls: Democrats Lead Key Senate Races In Last New York Times Poll

article: Today is election day in the United States. Voters choose all 435 members of the House of Representatives, 35 senators and 36 governors, plus most state legislatures and 145 statewide ballot questions[^12][^13]. More than 54 million ballots were cast early, about nine million more than at the same point in 2022, according to AP figures cited by Fox News[^13].

Control of Congress is at stake. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats; in the House, Democrats need a net gain of three[^12][^13]. Final New York Times/Siena polls show Democratic Senate candidates ahead in Texas, Kansas and Michigan, while a separate poll has Nebraska tied[^14]. The betting market Kalshi gives Democrats about a 94% chance of winning the House[^14]. Polls and markets are estimates, not results.

The parties tell different stories. President Trump predicts Republicans will keep both chambers, and the Republican chair says turnout will decide it[^13]. The Democratic chair says his party can flip both[^13]. Fox News lists the headwinds Republicans face: inflation, an unpopular war with Iran and falling approval ratings[^13].

Some ballot questions could matter beyond this year, including a one-time 5% tax on billionaires in California, new district maps in Maryland and Missouri, abortion measures in three states, and Alaska's vote on dropping ranked-choice voting[^12][^13].

Why it matters for Canada: Congress shapes trade, tariffs and support for Ukraine. What next: polls close between 6 p.m. and 1 a.m. Eastern, and close Senate races such as Alaska, Maine and Nebraska may take days[^13]. My read: if Democrats win even one chamber, the second half of Trump's term becomes harder for the White House.

topics.heading: Poland's fight over its top court becomes a standoff, and three ambassadors quit
topics.summary: Poland's government and president are locked in a struggle over who controls the Constitutional Tribunal, including a late-night confrontation at the court. Three ambassadors resigned, and the European Commission backed parliament's right to appoint judges.[^15][^17]

lead.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court

alsoReported.title: Polish PM Donald Tusk urges president to confirm judges amid constitutional crisis
EU Commission: Polish Parliament has right to appoint judges to the Constitutional Court

article: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, the court that rules on whether laws fit the constitution, is at the centre of a power struggle. On Oct 30, eight judges chosen by parliament this year declared the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, suspended. He served in the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and called the move a "coup d'état"[^15]. Early on Oct 31, video showed President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, pushing past a judge who says she is the court's acting head[^18][^16].

The dispute goes back years. Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-EU government, in office since December 2023, does not recognise the court as it now stands and has not followed its rulings. The dispute dates to 2015, when the PiS government of the time named its own judges; this year parliament began filling the court's seats[^15]. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight new judges, even though the law says new judges take their oath before the president[^18][^15].

Each side accuses the other. Tusk says there can be "no compromise" on the rule of law and on Monday urged Nawrocki to recognise the judges[^15][^16]. PiS and its allies in Europe call the government's moves a coup[^17]. Many legal experts, including critics of PiS, doubt that the way the new judges took control was lawful[^15]. The European Commission says appointing the judges is within parliament's powers[^17]. Three ambassadors who once advised the former president resigned in protest, most recently Poland's envoy to the UN[^15].

Why it matters: Poland is one of the EU's largest members and a key backer of Ukraine. This is a judgment, but when a court becomes a prize in a political fight, people on both sides can lose trust that its rulings are fair. What next: the court's disputed acting head called a meeting of its judges for today, and a valid vote needs ten judges[^15].
topics.differences: The government and the European Commission say parliament has the right to appoint the new judges[^16][^17]. PiS, President Nawrocki's allies and the suspended chief justice call the takeover a coup[^15][^17]. Independent legal experts are split: many doubt the method used, even if they criticise PiS[^15]. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski suggests the ambassadors resigned at Nawrocki's urging[^15].

topics.heading: Ebola deaths pass 5,300 in the fastest-growing outbreak on record
topics.summary: Africa CDC says 5,376 people have died in the Ebola outbreak centred on Congo, with deaths also in Kenya and Uganda. The strain has no approved vaccine, and a trial of a related one has begun.[^19][^21]

lead.title: Ebola kills over 5,300 in fastest-growing outbreak on record

alsoReported.title: DR Congo: WHO urges sustained efforts as Ebola cases top 10,000
Nigerian Health Chiefs Confirm Negative Results in Ebola Cases

article: Africa CDC, the continent's disease-control agency, told AFP on Monday that 5,376 people have died in the current Ebola outbreak: 5,372 in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two each in Kenya and Uganda[^19]. Congo's figures show more than 10,000 infections since May, and more than half of known cases have died[^19]. The UN says it is Congo's largest Ebola outbreak and the second-largest ever, after West Africa in 2014-16[^21].

Ebola spreads through contact with the body fluids of sick or dead people. This outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, which has no approved vaccine or treatment[^19][^21]. On Oct 23, a trial began in Bunia using Ervebo, a vaccine approved for a different Ebola strain, given to close contacts of patients; WHO experts are also reviewing two vaccines designed for Bundibugyo[^21].

The virus has crossed borders. Kenya recorded its first-ever cases, nine with two deaths, all linked to one traveller from Congo[^19]. In Nigeria, two suspected cases tested negative on Monday; the country's only confirmed case was a traveller who has since returned to Switzerland[^20]. The Central African Republic has increased screening along its long border with Congo[^20].

Why it matters: eastern Congo has armed conflict and many displaced people, which makes tracing contacts and holding safe burials hard; a nurse was killed in Tshopo province on Oct 24[^21][^20]. WHO says more than 2,600 people have recovered and testing has expanded[^21]. What next: watch for WHO's verdict on the Bundibugyo vaccines, early results from the trial, and any spread to new countries.

topics.heading: AI shares keep swinging as investors question the data-centre spending boom
topics.summary: US tech stocks fell again on Monday while most other shares rose, as investors ask whether hundreds of billions of dollars spent on AI data centres will pay off.[^22][^23]

lead.title: THE CLOSING BELL: US stocks erase their rally from the morning as tech and AI stocks keep swinging

alsoReported.title: US tech selloff drags global stocks back into the red
Asian shares are mixed as tech losses offset broader gains on Wall Street

article: US stock markets had a split day on Monday. The S&P 500 fell 0.5% after rising early, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 1.1%, but the Dow rose 0.4% and seven in ten S&P 500 stocks outside tech gained[^22]. On Tuesday the selling reached Asia, where South Korea's main index fell 2.5% as chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung dropped[^24].

The worry is about spending. Big technology companies are pouring money into data centres, the huge buildings full of computers that train and run AI. Goldman Sachs expects big cloud companies' spending on such projects to nearly double to about $800 billion this year and reach $1.2 trillion in 2027[^23]. Some investors fear the revenue will not be large enough to justify that, and some call it a bubble[^22].

Recent results fed the doubts. On Oct 29 Alphabet, Google's parent company, had its worst day on record, falling more than 12% on worries about search growth and heavy spending[^22]. On Monday Oracle fell 8.6% on plans to raise $20 billion, and chipmaker Marvell fell about 13% after agreeing to buy Lumentum[^23]. Not every signal was negative: Anthropic's updated filing to sell shares to the public showed revenue up 47% from the previous quarter[^23].

Why it matters: when a few giant companies lose value, so do the pension funds and savings that hold them, and slower AI building would affect jobs, power demand and chip supply worldwide. What next: more company results and US jobs data this week. My read: one rough stretch does not prove a bubble, but investors now want evidence that AI pays.

question.text: Today's brief has several numbers that differ by outlet: the death toll in Komyshuvakha, the size of Monday's oil price drop, Ebola totals. When two reliable sources give different figures for the same event, what would you want to know before deciding which to use?
